topic: Usage metrics contrasted with value metrics after launch
stem: Ninety days after launch, an AI feature's weekly active usage is high and still rising. Why is that insufficient as a measure of post-launch success?

options.text: Usage counts are typically inflated by automated health checks and synthetic monitoring traffic hitting the same endpoints.
Usage shows that people are engaging with the feature, not that the engagement produced the outcome the work was funded to deliver.
Usage cannot be compared across teams, because every team defines an active user slightly differently.
Usage is a lagging indicator, so by the time it moves in either direction the opportunity to intervene on the underlying cause has already passed.

explanation.correct: Adoption is a precondition for value, not evidence of it. A feature can be used constantly and still save nobody any time, because users verify its output twice, or because the saving it creates is consumed by a downstream step. The business case named an outcome — hours saved, error rate reduced, cycle time cut — and only that measurement, taken the same way it was forecast, closes the loop. High usage with an unmeasured outcome is the most common way a programme reports success it cannot substantiate.

distractors.A: Synthetic traffic contaminating usage counts is a real instrumentation defect and is fixed by filtering. Even a perfectly clean usage number would still not be a value number. Filtering synthetic traffic is instrumentation hygiene rather than an answer to the question asked.
distractors.C: Definitional inconsistency makes cross-team comparison awkward and is solved by agreeing a definition. It says nothing about whether usage measures the right thing in the first place. A single agreed definition would leave exactly the same gap between engagement and outcome.
distractors.D: Usage is if anything a leading indicator: it moves early, moves quickly, and is available within days of launch. The value measures are the ones that lag, which is precisely why teams substitute usage for them.

explanation.concept: Report a value metric alongside every adoption metric, and define the value metric before launch so it can be compared with the forecast. Adoption answers whether people will use it; value answers whether it was worth building. Programmes that track only the first cannot tell success from expensive habit.
explanation.tip: Whenever a stem offers a healthy-looking engagement number, ask what business quantity it was supposed to move. The gap between those two questions is what these items test.

topic: Human review capacity that does not scale from pilot
stem: A specialist lender piloted a Claude-based covenant-breach detector with two credit analysts reviewing every flagged case. The pilot covered 150 loans a week, flagged 11% of them, and each review took about 25 minutes. Production volume is 4,000 loans a week. The credit team has nine analysts with roughly 12 free hours each per week, headcount is frozen for the financial year, and the lender's credit policy requires every potential breach to be recorded and dispositioned. What does the production plan need?

options.text: Recruit the additional analyst capacity required to review every flagged case at production volume, and treat it as a running cost of the programme rather than a reason to redesign the control.
Raise the detection threshold until the number of flags fits comfortably inside the review hours the team already has available.
Reserve full review for a defined high-risk subset sized against the 108 available hours, with the remainder taking a lighter documented check.
Proceed with full review of every flag and manage the resulting queue, using queue age as the operational control and escalation trigger.

explanation.correct: Production flags run at 11% of 4,000, or 440 a week, and at 25 minutes each that is about 183 hours of review against 108 hours available. The pilot never tested this because 150 loans produced under seven hours of work, which two analysts absorbed without noticing. With headcount frozen and every potential breach required to be dispositioned, the only remaining variable is how much review each flag receives, so the plan must define a risk-based split and size the full-review tier to the capacity that actually exists.

distractors.A: The shortfall is around 75 hours a week, roughly two full-time analysts, and the stem states headcount is frozen for the year. A plan that depends on hiring that cannot happen is not a plan.
distractors.B: Suppressing flags to fit staffing means potential breaches are never recorded, which the credit policy forbids. It also sets a detection threshold from a resourcing constraint rather than from risk appetite, and hides the trade in a model parameter where nobody governs it.
distractors.D: A 75-hour weekly deficit produces a queue that grows without limit, so queue age will breach whatever threshold is set and keep going. Monitoring an unbounded backlog documents the failure rather than controlling it.

explanation.concept: Human review capacity scales with flag volume, not with model quality, and pilots almost never surface the constraint because pilot volume is small. Before promotion, compute review hours at production volume against real available hours, and if they do not fit, redesign the review model into risk-based tiers rather than suppressing detection or assuming headcount.
explanation.tip: Whenever a pilot puts a human in the loop, multiply the per-case review time by the production case rate before reading the options. The arithmetic usually shows the loop is the thing that does not scale.

topic: Purpose of drilling the runbook before handover
stem: What is the purpose of running a scheduled drill of an AI system's runbook before ownership transfers to a run team?

options.text: To satisfy the assurance requirement that operational documentation exists and has been formally reviewed and signed.
To benchmark the model's latency under load so that capacity planning can be finalised before go-live.
To give the receiving team exposure to the system's architecture and design rationale in a low-pressure setting.
To find the steps that do not work: missing access, stale commands, approvals nobody can grant out of hours.

explanation.correct: Runbooks are written by people who already have the access, know the flags and can get an approval by walking to a desk. Every one of those assumptions fails silently for the receiving team, and a drill is the only cheap way to discover which. The characteristic findings are mundane and fatal: a credential the run team does not hold, a command that only works from the build team's network, a rollback that needs a sign-off from someone who is not on any rota after six in the evening.

distractors.A: Documented-and-reviewed is an assurance checkbox that a drill happens to satisfy. Treating it as the purpose leads to drills designed to pass rather than to fail, which is where the value is.
distractors.B: Load and latency benchmarking is a performance test with a different design, different tooling and a different audience. A runbook drill exercises procedures, not throughput. A drill that produced a latency figure and no procedural defects would count as a wasted drill.
distractors.C: Architecture exposure is genuinely useful and is what a walkthrough delivers. A drill is deliberately narrower: it tests whether documented steps execute, not whether the team understands the design. Run both, and do not let the more comfortable one substitute for the other.

explanation.concept: Drill the runbook before handover, with the receiving team executing and the building team observing rather than helping. Score the drill on defects found in the procedure — access, commands, approvals, timing — and fix them while the original team is still available. A runbook that has never been executed by its intended reader is untested code.
explanation.tip: Ask what the activity is designed to produce. A drill produces a defect list; a walkthrough produces understanding; a load test produces numbers. The exam separates these three deliberately.

topic: Adjusting handover for a run team in another time zone
stem: A Nordic bank is transferring its Claude-based transaction-narrative service to a run team seven hours ahead, in a different legal entity. The two teams overlap for about two working hours a day. The build team will remain available for three months, then disband. Which two adjustments to the standard handover most directly address the time-zone and entity split? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Grant the run team's entity its own credentials and rollback approval rights, so no production action requires an approver who is asleep or in another company.
Extend the build team's availability from three months to twelve, so that the two-hour overlap constraint matters less during the transition and the run team can take its time.
Move the daily handover session into the two-hour overlap and use it for a live incident replay driven by the run team, not for status reporting.
Record video walkthroughs of every runbook procedure so the run team can watch them outside the overlap window.
Route all production alerts to both teams for the full three months so nothing can be missed while the run team builds confidence.

explanation.correct: The two structural problems are that approval chains cross both a time zone and a corporate boundary, and that only two hours a day of shared time exist. Delegating credentials and rollback authority to the receiving entity removes the dependency on a person who is unavailable for most of their working day. Spending the scarce overlap on the run team actually performing incident replays — rather than on a status call that could have been an email — converts the only synchronous hours into the practice the transfer depends on.

distractors.B: Extending availability buys calendar time and changes neither the two-hour overlap nor the authority split, so the same handover proceeds more slowly. It also removes the deadline that makes transfers complete.
distractors.D: Recorded walkthroughs are a reasonable asynchronous supplement and are worth producing. Watching someone else execute a procedure does not establish that the viewer can execute it, which is the gap a distributed handover most needs to close.
distractors.E: Dual alerting for three months feels safe and reliably produces the opposite: with two teams paged, each assumes the other has it, and the run team never experiences being the only responder. Overlap alerting should be short and end on a date.

explanation.concept: Distributed handovers fail on authority and on synchronous time. Give the receiving team the credentials and approval rights it needs to act alone, and spend the limited overlap on supervised execution rather than reporting. Dual ownership of alerting should be brief and dated, because shared responsibility for a page is no responsibility.
explanation.tip: Count the true-and-responsive options against the two constraints the stem names. Recording videos and extending support are generically helpful, which is what makes them the standard over-selection here.

topic: Transferring the evaluation suite with the system
stem: Why must the evaluation suite transfer to the run team along with a production Claude system?

options.text: Without it the run team cannot tell whether a change or a fix is safe to deploy, so every subsequent change becomes a guess.
Evaluation results are required evidence for the organisation's annual audit of automated decision systems.
The evaluation suite is in practice the only place where the system's functional requirements have been written down in a form that can actually be executed and checked.
A model version cannot be pinned or migrated without an evaluation record accompanying the configuration.

explanation.correct: A run team does not only watch a system; it changes one. It applies fixes, reverts, adjusts prompts and eventually migrates the model version, and for a probabilistic system none of those can be validated by reading the diff. The evaluation suite is the instrument that turns a proposed change into a decision, so a team that inherits the system without it has responsibility for something it cannot safely modify. That is why the suite has to run in their pipeline, on their infrastructure, before the transfer closes.

distractors.B: Audit evidence is a real use of evaluation results in regulated settings and is a secondary benefit. The suite would still have to transfer in an organisation with no such audit, because the operational need is independent of it.
distractors.C: Requirements ought to be documented elsewhere as well, and in many systems they are. Even where the suite is the best statement of intent, its operational value is as an instrument rather than as a specification.
distractors.D: Nothing prevents pinning or migrating a version without an evaluation record; teams do it and regret it. The claim states a good practice as a technical constraint. Providers do not inspect your evaluation practice before honouring a version pin.

explanation.concept: Hand over the instrument, not just the artefact. A run team inheriting an AI system needs the evaluation suite running in its own pipeline, the golden dataset it depends on, and the thresholds that constitute a pass. Without them the team can restart the service but cannot safely change it, which is most of what running a system involves.
explanation.tip: Ask what the receiving team will need to do next month, not next week. Monitoring needs dashboards; changing anything needs evals, and every system gets changed.

topic: Acting on a benefit shortfall located by a time study
stem: Six months after launch, a wholesaler's Claude-based order-entry assistant shows 88% adoption and all quality metrics inside target, yet the forecast saving of 6 minutes per order has materialised as 1.4 minutes. A time-and-motion study finds the assistant does save 6 minutes on drafting, but staff now spend 4.6 minutes reconciling its output into the ERP by hand because the assistant cannot write to it. The study attributes that time to manual re-keying, not to correcting errors. What should the team do?

options.text: Report the realised 1.4-minute saving, revise the business case downward, and record the programme as delivering a smaller but genuine benefit.
Invest in raising the assistant's accuracy so that staff have less to reconcile when they transfer output into the ERP.
Prioritise the ERP write integration, since that is where the forecast benefit is being consumed, and re-read the benefit once it ships.
Retire the assistant, because a 1.4-minute saving per order does not justify the ongoing run cost and the change management overhead.

explanation.correct: The study has done something unusual and valuable: it has located the leak precisely. Six minutes are created and 4.6 are destroyed by a single missing integration, and the stem rules out quality as the cause by attributing the time to re-keying rather than correction. That makes the remedy a bounded piece of engineering with a known payoff of up to 4.6 minutes per order, which is a far better return than anything else on the backlog. Re-reading the benefit after it ships closes the loop the review opened.

distractors.A: Accepting the shortfall is honest and premature. Revising the business case is right once you have exhausted the fix; doing it while a quantified, addressable cause sits in the report writes off most of the benefit voluntarily.
distractors.B: Accuracy work would be the answer if the reconciliation time were spent correcting errors, and the study explicitly says it is not. Improving a metric that is already inside target while the actual bottleneck is manual transcription spends effort where there is nothing to gain.
distractors.D: Retirement discards a system that demonstrably creates six minutes of value per order and is losing it downstream. The run cost argument is being made against the wrong number. Retirement would also return staff to drafting from scratch, giving back the six minutes the assistant creates.

explanation.concept: When realised benefit falls short of forecast, instrument the end-to-end task rather than the component. Benefits are usually not absent but displaced into a step nobody counted — a manual re-key, a second review, a reconciliation. Fix the displacement before revising the business case, and re-measure the same way the forecast was made.
explanation.tip: Follow the arithmetic in the stem: six minutes created, 4.6 consumed, 1.4 left. When a shortfall decomposes that cleanly, the item is asking you to remove the consumer, not to renegotiate the forecast.

topic: Why user reports understate the production failure rate
stem: Why do user-reported issues systematically understate an AI system's production failure rate?

options.text: Because the system logs its own failures separately from the user reporting channel, and the two counts are never reconciled.
Because users cannot report a failure they did not notice, and confidently wrong output is precisely the failure that does not announce itself.
Because most production failures occur outside core hours, when fewer users are active to observe them.
Because users who are unsure about an output tend to file a report anyway, which inflates rather than deflates the recorded count and buries the genuine failures among them.

explanation.correct: Reporting requires detection, and the characteristic AI failure is output that reads exactly like a correct answer. A user who cannot tell that a summary omitted a clause or that a figure was invented has nothing to report, and reports nothing. The undercount is therefore not random noise but is concentrated in exactly the failures that matter most. This is why production quality has to be sampled and audited independently, rather than inferred from the volume of complaints.

distractors.A: Unreconciled counts are an instrumentation and process gap worth closing, and reconciling them would not reveal the undetected failures, because neither channel contains them. Neither the log nor the report channel records an error the system did not know it had made.
distractors.C: There is no general reason for AI quality failures to cluster outside core hours; if anything they follow traffic. The claim invents a pattern to explain a real effect. Even if it were true, that would shift when reports arrive rather than how many failures exist.
distractors.D: This asserts the opposite of the observed behaviour. Uncertain users tend to resolve their own doubt and move on rather than file a report, which is part of why the undercount exists.

explanation.concept: Never treat complaint volume as a quality metric for an AI system. Detection is a filter and it is biased toward the failures users can see, so pair reporting channels with independent sampling and audit of production output. A falling report rate can mean improving quality or eroding vigilance, and only sampling distinguishes them.
explanation.tip: Ask what a failure has to do in order to become a report. If it has to be noticed by someone who cannot easily verify the answer, the reported rate is a floor and not an estimate.

topic: Rationalising duplicate AI systems after an acquisition
stem: An insurer acquires a competitor. Both operate a Claude-based first-notice-of-loss triage assistant. The acquirer's handles 9,000 claims a month and has a documented evaluation suite, a pinned model version and a named run team. The acquired one handles 3,500 a month, has no evaluation suite, and is tightly coupled to the acquired company's policy administration system, whose own migration is a separate programme expected to take at least three years. The integration lead proposes retiring the acquired assistant immediately. What should the architect advise?

options.text: Retire the acquired assistant now and route its 3,500 claims a month to the acquirer's assistant, funding the necessary policy-system integration work as a one-off cost of the merger.
Keep both systems permanently, since each is coupled to a different policy administration platform and neither dependency is going away soon.
Build a single new assistant that serves both policy systems and retire both existing ones once it reaches parity with each.
Bring the acquired assistant under the acquirer's operating model — evaluation suite, pinned version, run-team ownership — and tie its sunset date to the policy-system migration.

explanation.correct: The acquired assistant cannot be retired before the system it is coupled to, and that dependency is a three-year programme owned elsewhere. What can change immediately is that it is running in production with no evaluation suite, no version discipline and no accountable operator, which is the real risk. Adopting it into the acquirer's operating model closes that gap now, while binding its sunset date to the policy migration keeps it from becoming permanent and makes the retirement someone's tracked commitment rather than an aspiration.

distractors.A: This treats a three-year platform migration as a one-off integration cost. The coupling is to a policy administration system that is being replaced on its own multi-year schedule, and no amount of funding on the assistant collapses that timeline.
distractors.B: Permanence is the failure mode of post-merger duplication: two systems, two operating models, and no date on which anyone has to resolve it. The technical dependency justifies coexistence for a period, not forever.
distractors.C: A greenfield unified assistant means building a third system while two run, reaching parity twice, and migrating twice. It is the option that looks strategic and maximises the number of systems in flight.

explanation.concept: When duplicate AI systems survive a merger because of dependencies you do not control, separate two decisions. Governance is adopted immediately: evaluation suite, version pinning, ownership, monitoring, on all inherited systems. Retirement is scheduled against the dependency that blocks it, with a named date and owner, so coexistence stays temporary.
explanation.tip: Split what can be fixed now from what is gated by someone else's programme. The stem's three-year dependency eliminates every option that retires or replaces quickly, leaving the question of what to do in the meantime.

topic: Shipping a base prompt change under tenant customisation
stem: A B2B SaaS vendor's Claude-based support-ticket classifier lets each of 700 tenants append custom instructions to a shared base prompt. The vendor wants to change the base prompt to improve category precision. The evaluation suite exercises the base prompt alone, with no tenant instructions attached. What should the vendor do before shipping?

options.text: Evaluate the new base against a volume-stratified sample of real tenant instruction sets, then roll out by tenant cohort against a quality threshold.
Ship to all tenants at once, since the base prompt is the vendor's to change under the terms of service, and tenant instructions are appended after it rather than mixed into it.
Ask all 700 tenants to re-test their own instruction sets in a sandbox and confirm acceptance before the change is applied to their environment.
Freeze tenant custom instructions for the duration of the change so the variable is eliminated, then unfreeze once the new base is stable.

explanation.correct: The deployed artefact is not the base prompt; it is 700 combinations of base plus tenant text, and instructions interact rather than compose cleanly. A suite that tests the base alone therefore tests a configuration no tenant runs. Sampling real instruction sets stratified by volume puts the largest tenants and the widest variety of instruction styles into the evaluation, and cohort rollout against a threshold catches the interactions the sample missed while the affected population is still small.

distractors.B: Appending is a textual arrangement, not an isolation guarantee: a base instruction and a tenant instruction can conflict, and the model resolves the conflict in ways nobody specified. Ownership of the base prompt settles who may change it, not whether the change is safe.
distractors.C: Asking 700 tenants to validate a vendor change transfers the vendor's testing obligation to its customers, and most will not respond. The rollout then stalls behind non-responses or proceeds without the confirmations it claimed to require.
distractors.D: Freezing customisation removes tenants' ability to respond to their own operational needs and would itself be a breaking change to the product. It also postpones rather than answers the question of how the combined prompts behave.

explanation.concept: Evaluate the configuration you actually deploy. Where users or tenants contribute part of the prompt, the evaluation set must sample real contributed text, stratified so that high-volume and unusual cases are represented, and rollout must be staged by cohort with a quality gate. Testing the vendor-controlled fragment alone tests a system nobody runs.
explanation.tip: Look for the gap between what the eval suite covers and what production actually executes. In multi-tenant and user-configurable systems that gap is the item, and options about ownership or freezing are avoiding it.

topic: Authority that must accompany run-team responsibility
stem: A run team has been given responsibility for a production Claude system. What must accompany that responsibility for the arrangement to work at three in the morning?

options.text: A documented service level agreement with each business unit that consumes the system's output.
Authority to roll back the prompt and model version and to disable the feature, without seeking the build team's approval.
A dedicated budget line covering the system's inference spend and the supporting infrastructure, owned by the run team's own cost centre.
Read access to the source repository, the prompt registry and the latest evaluation results.

explanation.correct: Responsibility without authority is a pager with no controls attached. The actions that stop harm in an AI system are reverting the prompt, reverting the model version and turning the feature off, and if any of them requires an approver who is asleep then the run team's real capability at three in the morning is to wake someone up. Delegating those rights, with the conditions under which they may be used written into the runbook, is what makes the ownership transfer real rather than nominal.

distractors.A: Service level agreements define what the run team owes consumers. They are worth having and they do not give anyone the ability to act during an incident. Consumers are also not served during an incident by a team that must phone someone for permission.
distractors.C: Budget ownership should transfer too, and it governs decisions taken over months. It has no bearing on what the on-call engineer can do in the next five minutes. Cost ownership should transfer with the system, and it belongs to a different conversation from incident authority.
distractors.D: Read access lets the team see what is deployed and diagnose the problem. Diagnosis without the right to change anything simply produces a better-informed escalation. The run team already held read access throughout the shadowing period and still could not act alone.

explanation.concept: Transfer authority with responsibility: rollback rights, feature disablement, and pre-authorised conditions for using them, all held by the team carrying the pager. Document the boundary — what they may do unilaterally, what requires escalation — so the decision is made in advance rather than during the incident.
explanation.tip: Test each option by asking whether it changes what the on-call engineer can do in the next five minutes. Agreements, budgets and read access all fail that test.

topic: First live incident during a supervised handover period
stem: A utility's run team is four weeks into an eight-week shadowing handover of a Claude-based outage-notification drafter, with the build team still on call as backup. At 21:40 the drafter begins producing customer messages that name the wrong substations. The runbook's rollback is a single command. The run-team engineer on shift has never executed a rollback in production and this step has not yet been drilled. The build team's on-call engineer answers the phone immediately. What is the next step?

options.text: The build-team engineer performs the rollback, since customer-facing messages are already wrong and the run-team engineer has never run the procedure.
The run-team engineer escalates to the product owner to confirm that incorrect substation names justify a rollback before anything is changed.
The build-team engineer stays on the line while the run-team engineer executes the rollback, and the undrilled step goes to the handover review.
The run-team engineer disables the drafter entirely and leaves the rollback for the build team to perform during business hours tomorrow.

explanation.correct: A supervised handover period exists precisely so the receiving team's first production action happens with an expert on the line rather than after they have gone. The rollback is one command and the build engineer is already reachable, so supervised execution costs seconds and produces an engineer who has now done it. Taking over would resolve this incident and leave the run team in exactly the same state for the next one, four weeks before the backup disappears.

distractors.A: This is the instinct under pressure and it is the one the shadowing period is designed to resist. With a single-command rollback and the expert on the call, the marginal delay is negligible against the marginal value of the run team having performed it once.
distractors.B: Wrong substation names in outage notifications to customers is not a judgement call requiring the product owner, and the runbook should already say so. Escalating for permission adds delay while incorrect messages continue to go out.
distractors.D: Disabling the drafter means no outage notifications are produced at all during an outage, which is worse for customers than a targeted rollback. It also defers the action the run team most needs to practise.

explanation.concept: Use the supervised handover window deliberately: the receiving team acts and the departing team advises, on real incidents, while the safety net still exists. Every incident that the build team resolves on the run team's behalf is a rehearsal spent, and undrilled runbook steps discovered in an incident belong in the handover review as findings.
explanation.tip: When a stem carefully tells you the rollback is one command and the expert is reachable, it has removed the speed argument for taking over. What remains is who should be able to do this next month.

topic: Re-baselining monitoring after a model version migration
stem: After migrating a production system from one pinned model version to its successor, why must monitoring baselines be re-established?

options.text: Because the metrics recorded against the previous version are discarded when the pin is changed.
Because alert thresholds are stored against the model version identifier in the monitoring configuration and do not carry across a version migration.
Because the successor's rate limits differ, which changes the shape of the observed error-rate series.
Because thresholds tuned to the old version's output distribution will either fire constantly or stop firing, and both leave you blind.

explanation.correct: Quality-proxy thresholds are empirical: refusal rate, average output length, tool-call frequency, escalation rate and groundedness-check pass rate were all tuned to what the previous version did. A successor with a different output distribution shifts every one of them. Left alone, the alerts either scream continuously until the team mutes them or sit permanently silent because the new normal is inside the band, and in both cases the migration has quietly removed the team's ability to detect a real regression.

distractors.A: Historical metrics remain in the observability store and are exactly what you use to compare the two versions. Nothing is discarded when a pin changes. Comparing the two series is in fact the main input to setting the new thresholds.
distractors.B: Thresholds live in the monitoring configuration and are not attached to a provider version identifier. The problem is that they carry over unchanged when they should not. Even where tooling tags alerts by version, the numeric threshold inside them still has to be re-derived.
distractors.C: Throughput and limit behaviour may differ and would show up as capacity work. That is not why quality thresholds stop being meaningful. Capacity behaviour and output-distribution behaviour are separate concerns with separate alerts, and only the second is invalidated by a version change.

explanation.concept: A model migration invalidates every empirically tuned threshold. Plan the migration to include a re-baselining period: run the successor long enough to characterise its output distribution, reset thresholds against it, and keep the old series for comparison. Until thresholds are reset, treat the system as unmonitored on quality rather than as healthy.
explanation.tip: Distinguish an alert that cannot fire from an alert that fires constantly. Both are silence, and a migration produces one or the other on every threshold nobody revisited.

topic: Sustaining enablement in a high-turnover population
stem: A contact centre with 45% annual agent turnover rolled out a Claude-based response assistant to 600 agents through a one-off classroom programme delivered over six weeks. Six months later, quality audit scores among agents hired since the programme are materially below those of agents who attended it. Which two changes address the cause? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Repeat the six-week classroom programme once a year, so that every cohort of joiners eventually receives the same full training the original population did.
Fold the assistant module into the standard new-hire induction curriculum, owned by the training function rather than the project team.
Require team leaders to attest that each new joiner has read the assistant guidance before taking live calls.
Embed the key checks as in-product guidance at the moment the agent reviews the assistant's output.
Publish the training deck on the intranet and email the link to each new joiner on their first day.

explanation.correct: The cause is structural: enablement was delivered as a project event to a population that turns over almost half every year, so the trained proportion decays continuously. Moving the module into induction, owned by the function that runs induction permanently, makes coverage automatic for everyone who arrives. In-product guidance is the complement, because it does not depend on anyone having been trained at all and it appears at the moment the check is needed rather than months earlier.

distractors.A: An annual repeat leaves an agent hired the week after it runs untrained for up to a year, which in a 45%-turnover population is most of the joiners. It also re-spends the full programme cost each time.
distractors.E: Publishing and emailing a deck is distribution, not enablement. First-day email is also the least-read message a new joiner receives, competing with payroll, systems access and compliance modules. It also arrives on the day a new joiner is least able to absorb anything.
distractors.C: Attestation records that something was read and produces no evidence of capability. It shifts accountability to team leaders without giving them anything that changes an agent's behaviour. The attestation is also taken before the joiner has seen a single real piece of assistant output.

explanation.concept: In a high-turnover population, project-delivered training decays toward zero coverage. Enablement must be transferred into a permanent owner's standing process — induction and onboarding — and reinforced by in-workflow guidance that works for users who received no training. Measure coverage as a proportion of current staff, not as attendance at a past event.
explanation.tip: When a stem gives you a turnover rate alongside a one-off training programme, the decay is the point. Options that repeat the event, or distribute material, leave the decay running.

topic: Release note content for a shared service behaviour change
stem: A platform team is shipping a prompt change to a shared Claude-based service consumed by several downstream teams. Beyond stating that behaviour has changed, what should the release note tell those teams?

options.text: Which output characteristics changed, on which input classes, and what each consuming team should re-test.
The full text of the previous and new prompts, so that consuming teams can diff them and reach their own conclusions.
The evaluation scores before and after the change, so teams can judge for themselves whether it was an improvement.
The rationale for the change and the stakeholder who requested it, so teams know where to direct questions.

explanation.correct: A downstream team's only question is whether this change breaks them, and answering it requires knowing what moved and where. Characterising the change by input class lets each consumer decide whether their traffic is affected, and naming what to re-test converts the note into a task they can schedule. This is work the platform team is uniquely able to do, because only it has run the evaluation across the full input space; leaving consumers to infer it means most of them will not.

distractors.B: A prompt diff shows what was written, not what changed in behaviour, and consumers cannot derive the second from the first. It also invites downstream teams to build dependencies on internal prompt wording.
distractors.C: Aggregate evaluation scores describe the platform team's test population, which is not any individual consumer's traffic. A score that improved overall can easily have regressed on one consumer's input class.
distractors.D: Rationale and a named contact are useful courtesy and belong in the note. Neither helps a consuming team work out whether its own integration still functions. A consuming team that reads only the rationale will conclude the change does not concern it.

explanation.concept: Write release notes for a shared AI service from the consumer's decision, not the producer's activity. State the behavioural delta by input class, name the re-test each consumer should run, and give the rollback and cutover dates. Prompt diffs and aggregate scores describe your work; consumers need a description of their exposure.
explanation.tip: Grade communication options by whether the reader can act on them. If a downstream engineer would still have to reverse-engineer the impact on their own traffic, the note has not done its job.

topic: Stopping iteration when gains fall inside measurement noise
stem: A charity's Claude-based donor-correspondence drafter has been through eight iterations in ten months. Each of the last three raised the internal quality score by under one point on a 100-point scale, while the team's own estimate of sampling noise on that score is about two points. Volunteers who use the drafter daily report no perceptible difference across those three releases. The product owner has asked for a ninth iteration on the same axis. What should the architect advise?

options.text: Continue, since small gains compound over time and the score remains well below the maximum the scale allows.
Increase the evaluation sample size until sub-point improvements can be resolved reliably, then resume iterating on the same axis.
Stop iterating on this axis, because the measured gains sit inside the instrument's noise, and move the effort to an axis where a difference would be observable.
Replace the internal quality score with a model-graded rubric that is more sensitive to small differences between releases.

explanation.correct: Three releases have produced movements smaller than the noise on the measurement, which means the team cannot distinguish improvement from resampling, and the users who would notice a real difference report none. Both lines of evidence agree that this axis is exhausted at the current level of effort. The right response is to redirect capacity to something whose effect would be visible — a new capability, a cost reduction, a latency improvement — rather than to keep buying changes nobody can detect.

distractors.A: Compounding requires that each increment is real, and the stem says these are indistinguishable from noise. Distance from the top of an arbitrary internal scale is not evidence that headroom exists in anything users experience.
distractors.B: A bigger sample would let the team resolve sub-point differences, at the cost of a longer, more expensive evaluation cycle to detect changes the users cannot perceive. It improves the instrument to keep measuring something that has stopped mattering.
distractors.D: Changing the grader mid-programme breaks comparability with the previous eight iterations and cannot make an imperceptible improvement perceptible. Higher sensitivity to differences users do not notice measures the wrong thing more precisely.

explanation.concept: Iterate until the gains fall inside the noise of your measurement or below the threshold users can perceive, then change axis. Diminishing returns on a quality metric are a signal to reallocate, not a signal to buy a finer instrument. Track effort per unit of realised, perceptible improvement so the exhaustion point is visible before eight iterations have passed.
explanation.tip: Compare the reported gain against the stated noise. When the gain is smaller, every option about measuring more precisely is a distractor, because precision cannot manufacture an effect that is not there.

topic: Purpose of a champion network during rollout
stem: What is the primary purpose of a superuser or champion network during the rollout of an AI assistant?

options.text: To reduce the training budget by delegating formal instruction to volunteers instead of professional trainers.
To place a credible local source of help, and of realistic expectations, next to each user group.
To give the programme team a controlled group on which to test new prompt versions before wider release.
To create a governance forum with authority to approve changes to the assistant's behaviour.

explanation.correct: Champions work because of who they are rather than what they know. A peer who does the same job, has used the tool on real cases, and will say plainly what it is bad at is believed in a way that programme communications are not. That credibility is what sets realistic expectations, and proximity is what makes the help usable — a question answered at the next desk in a minute is asked, where a ticket to a central team is not.

distractors.A: Champion networks cost time rather than saving it: the champions need earlier and deeper enablement than anyone else. Treating them as a cheap substitute for training produces under-prepared volunteers giving confident wrong answers.
distractors.C: An early-access cohort for testing releases is a different construct with a different selection rule, and volunteers make a biased test population. Champions may happen to see changes early, but that is not why they exist.
distractors.D: Behaviour changes are approved by whoever owns the system. Turning a support network into an approval body slows change and puts the decision with people who have no view of the evaluation results.

explanation.concept: Champion networks solve credibility and proximity, not cost or governance. Select champions for peer standing rather than enthusiasm, enable them earlier and more deeply than the general population, give them a direct route back to the product team, and recognise the time it takes them.
explanation.tip: When an option reframes a change-management structure as a cost saving or a decision-making body, treat it as wrong. These networks exist to make the message believable at the front line.

topic: Introducing phasing under a single-milestone contract
stem: A city transport authority's contract with its systems integrator specifies one acceptance milestone for a Claude-based journey-disruption assistant: accepted or not on a single date following a two-week user acceptance test, with payment tied to that milestone. The architect wants phased delivery to limit exposure. The contract cannot be reopened this financial year. What should the architect do?

options.text: Deliver internally in phases and present only the final phase as the contractual acceptance deliverable, keeping the milestone untouched.
Accept the single milestone and mitigate by extending user acceptance testing from two weeks to six with a broader tester population.
Ask the authority to waive acceptance for the first release and take the system provisionally while phasing is arranged informally.
Keep the milestone and phase technically inside it: ship behind a flag, enable progressively by user group against pre-agreed criteria, with a rollback the authority controls.

explanation.correct: The contract constrains when the authority formally accepts the system; it does not constrain how many users are exposed to it on any given day. Shipping the accepted release with the feature behind a flag preserves the milestone exactly as written while turning go-live into a sequence of controlled enablements with criteria and a rollback the customer can invoke. That gives the risk reduction phasing exists to provide without touching a commercial instrument that cannot be reopened.

distractors.A: Internal phasing improves how the integrator builds and changes nothing about exposure, because the whole user population still receives the system at once on acceptance day. The risk the architect is trying to manage lives after the milestone, not before it.
distractors.B: A longer acceptance test with more testers finds more defects, and it is still a test: nobody is doing real work with real consequences. It also delays the milestone that the payment is tied to, which is a commercial conversation of its own.
distractors.C: Provisional acceptance is a contract change by another name, and it removes the authority's protection while giving it nothing in return. It is unlikely to be agreed and would leave the integrator delivering against no defined gate.

explanation.concept: Contractual acceptance and operational exposure are separate levers. When procurement forces a single acceptance event, achieve phasing technically — feature flags, progressive enablement by cohort, pre-agreed enablement criteria and a customer-controlled kill switch — so risk is staged even though the commercial milestone is not.
explanation.tip: When a stem says a contract cannot be reopened, discard every option that negotiates. The question is what you can do inside the constraint, and flags decouple exposure from acceptance.

topic: Assets to preserve when replacing a system with a vendor product
stem: A retailer is retiring its in-house Claude-based product-description generator after two years and moving to a vendor SaaS product. The team is preparing to archive the repository and shut the service down. Which two assets should be preserved and transferred to the team adopting the vendor product? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: The evaluation set and rubric built from two years of production failures, the only instrument that can test whether the vendor product is at least as good.
The prompt library, so the incoming team can paste the same instructions into the vendor product's configuration screens rather than rewrite them for its own controls.
The complete conversation logs of every generation request served over the two years of operation, exported to the retailer's archive.
The catalogue of known failure modes and product categories where output was consistently weak, so the vendor product is tested against them before cutover.
The infrastructure-as-code definitions and deployment pipelines that built and released the retiring generator service.

explanation.correct: Two years of production taught the retailer things about this task that no vendor demonstration will reveal: which product categories are hard, where output goes wrong, and what a good description looks like for their catalogue. That knowledge is embodied in the evaluation set and in the failure-mode catalogue, and both are portable because they describe the task rather than the implementation. They are also the only means of testing the vendor's claim of equivalence against the retailer's own bar rather than the vendor's.

distractors.B: Prompts are written against a specific model, interface and surrounding scaffolding, and a vendor product will expose different configuration entirely. Pasting them in is unlikely to work and encourages the new team to skip building an understanding of the vendor's own controls.
distractors.E: Deployment pipelines for a service being shut down have no consumer. The vendor product is operated through its own interfaces, so this is infrastructure for a system that will not exist.
distractors.C: Bulk logs with no curation are storage cost and retention exposure rather than an asset. Their value has already been extracted into the evaluation set and the failure catalogue, which is what makes those two the things worth keeping.

explanation.concept: When replacing a system, the durable assets are the task knowledge, not the implementation. Evaluation sets, golden datasets and failure-mode catalogues describe the problem and transfer to any successor, including a vendor product; prompts, pipelines and raw logs describe the solution you are discarding. Preserve the instrument that measures success before the code that produced it.
explanation.tip: Sort candidate assets into what is about the task and what is about the build. Only the first survives a change of implementation, and vendor migrations are exactly where teams throw away the wrong half.
